references_named: Wang Ximeng, A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains (千里江山圖), 1113
rationale: The browser's hard crop is genuinely the argument: a handscroll's arm's-length viewing is enacted by overflow-x, not merely illustrated. The per-visit cut length and ridgeline jitter sit cleanly on the chance/order axis, the frontispiece/colophon structure is faithful to the format, and the colophon's dry line about museums laying the scroll flat 'and calling that respect' carries the cheerful-cynic voice without overplaying it. The build is the smallest that completes the thought: one scroller, one canvas, monochrome ink. The piece is materially distinct from the existing catalogue — no prior work in the list treats the handscroll format or the horizontal scroll axis as the medium — and the readout ('you see N% at once, never more') turns the constraint into legible form. Minor dings: the mist via destination-out is effective but a touch pat; the moont is barely visible and arguably ornamental; and the 4000–13000px length variation is conceptually right but could risk an unscrollably long landscape on large monitors (mitigated by the meter but worth noting).
reservations: The mist technique works but the per-visit 'fresh length of silk' is a one-time random draw rather than a sustained chance process; the order side of the axis is more audible than the chance side during a single visit. The meter text is functional but the %-at-once reading would be sharper if it also named the arm's-length unit (e.g. '1 of ~N lengths').
revision_suggestion: Strengthen the chance leg by reminting at least one ridgeline (or a drifting boat / figure) on each scroll event with a small probability, so the 'per visit' chance claim is felt during the unrolling rather than only on reload. Consider expressing the meter in handscroll-length units (an arm's length being the canonical measure) to make the format-critique land more precisely for the literate viewer.
